name: The Refusal of Angles

detectability.signature: Starfield folds into repeating self-intersecting arcs; rangefinders return negative distances and parallax measurements contradict themselves

proximity: Navigation instruments deliver contradictory readings, each internally consistent
Distant ships appear to occupy several positions at once, all equally convincing
Straight-line courses visibly curve without any acceleration
contact: Vessels exit at locations unrelated to their entry vector, sometimes light-hours off
Crews report seeing the interior of their own hulls from outside while remaining aboard
prolonged_exposure: Dimensional displacement: crews return wrong, mirrored or missing members
Reality breakdown in ship systems as local geometry stops supporting stable structures

phenomena: Impossible geometries visible within: corridors of stars that fold back on themselves
Visible distortion of the starfield into repeating, self-crossing arcs
Ships exiting at different locations than entered, regardless of course flown
Objects appearing larger or smaller than their true dimensions depending on viewing angle
hazards: Dimensional displacement of vessel or crew during geometry shifts
Navigation system failure so complete that dead reckoning becomes fiction
Structural stress as hull geometry is briefly reinterpreted
opportunities: Access to otherwise unreachable regions glimpsed through folded sightlines
Test exotic theories of spacetime topology with unmatched precision
Ambush point for those who learn its exits; pursuit rarely follows correctly
known_incidents: The clipper Thessaly entered on a straight course and exited eleven hours later flying backward, her crew certain they had never turned
Four probes dispatched during the same geometry shift returned as five; the extra probe matched the others exactly and transmitted until decommissioned
description: At forty-eight thousand kilometers across, The Refusal of Angles looks at first like a lensing artifact: a patch of sky where the stars bend into graceful, self-crossing arcs. Look longer and the arcs resolve into structure, corridors of light that turn corners without angles and meet themselves from behind. Rangefinders return negative numbers with quiet confidence.

The zone pulses on a rough eleven-hour cycle, its interior geometry rearranging between states that each obey their own consistent rules and none obey ours. A ship flying dead straight may exit sideways, behind herself, or nowhere at all; the clipper Thessaly came out flying backward and swore she had never turned. Within the boundary, parallel lines are an opinion and distance is negotiable.

Her discovery is credited to the Thessaly incident, though fishermen's charts had marked a cursed region there for two centuries prior. The four-probes-returning-as-five affair remains the field's most cited embarrassment and its most cited evidence. Geometers have mapped seven distinct interior geometries and suspect at least twice that number.

Transit is possible and occasionally even deliberate, since certain fold-states offer passage to places no honest route reaches. Warning buoys track the pulse cycle, which drifts unpredictably enough to keep navigators humble. Most traffic gives it room; a few specialists study its exits, and fewer still are comfortable discussing what they see when the angles refuse.
